tasks.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); Results, 6th paragraph; Table 3 (p. 4)
tasks.extracted: 336 result sheets (1680 results) were returned by 218 unique participants, for a 5 CAD honorarium, with no follow-up of kits not returned; Table 3 counts 206 sheets filled in from recall at return and 122 completed at the time of testing, while the text gives the reverse. Editors' calculation: 206 of 328 sheets (63%) from recall.

The authors infer from the similar opioid positivity that people who use drugs can use the strips accurately with minimal training; they judge the stimulant divergence more likely to reflect the testing method (false positives) than differently contaminated supplies, and name as limitations the assumption of no systematic difference between the samples tested by the two groups and the lack of a design in which the same sample is tested by the person and by an expert.
tasks.quote: PWUD can accurately use fentanyl test strips with minimal training

tasks.locator: Abstract › Results; Methods › Data sources and searches; Results › Acceptability of FTS use by community, 1st paragraph; Feasibility of FTS Use, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Scoping review of 91 articles on fentanyl test strips (three databases searched on March 7, 2023; English only; mostly North American; no randomized trials; included studies not appraised): stated willingness to use strips ranged from 43% to 85% in five studies, while documented use ranged from 1% to 80% (median 19%; per-study values in a supplement not read).

tasks.locator: Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Survey tools and testing kits, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Take-home kits of five strips were handed out with brief peer training at ten British Columbia harm-reduction sites from April to July 2019; no contact or demographic details were collected when kits were handed out and kits not returned were not followed up, so how many kits were used is unknown; 336 results sheets were returned.

tasks.locator: Results › Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 1st to 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Only two of the 91 articles discuss overdose-related outcomes. At a Vancouver overdose prevention site, 1% of visits included a check, mostly after use, and intended dose reduction went with lower odds of overdose (0.41) whatever the result (no intervals printed). A vending machine in Hamilton County, Ohio, dispensed 10,155 strips with naloxone and injection supplies in its first year; 105 surveyed clients reported 937 detections of fentanyl and 702 instances of discarding the drug or using less, and county overdose deaths fell by about 10% while Ohio's rose by about 5%, confounded by the naloxone from the same machine and without a control group. The review concludes that only limited data suggest strip use decreases overdose rates or overdose mortality.

tasks.locator: Methods › Survey tools and testing kits, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Results, 8th paragraph (p. 4)
tasks.extracted: Each participant was asked about actions in response to both a positive and a negative result, in standard questions not based on their own results; for a positive result, 6 of 336 answers (1.8%) reported a riskier response (1 using more or more quickly, 5 using alone) and 217 (64.6%) no change. Editors' observation: responses to a negative result are not reported in the Results. Editors' calculation: 6 of 336 is 1.8% (Wilson 95% CI 0.8–3.8%).

tasks.locator: Results › FTS accuracy and reliability, 1st paragraph; Acceptability of FTS use by community › Limitations of FTS in an evolving drug supply, 3rd paragraph (AM p. 4); Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (AM p. 5); Behavior Change from FTS Results, 7th paragraph (AM p. 7)
tasks.extracted: As relayed (studies not appraised): carfentanil, norcarfentanil and norfentanyl test negative on strips; strips give no information on xylazine, synthetic cannabinoids, phenacetin, levamisole or etizolam; difficulty interpreting results ranged from 3% to almost 34%; some people believed that the intensity of the line shows how pure the fentanyl is, or that a negative strip indicates xylazine (and a positive one excludes it); a few participants in two studies said they use or would use strips to use more or faster, one saying a negative result would mean doing a little more, and in one study six participants (1.8%) reported riskier behaviour after a positive result.

tasks.locator: Results › Behavior Change from FTS Results, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Overdose related outcomes after FTS use, 1st to 4th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: As relayed: a median of 55% (range 23–75%) reported any positive behaviour change across seven studies, while some used drugs as usual after a positive result because of withdrawal, tolerance, doubt about the result or wanting fentanyl. Only two of the 91 articles discuss overdose-related outcomes, neither with a control group; in the vending-machine evaluation, county overdose deaths fell by about 10% while Ohio's rose by about 5%, with naloxone dispensed by the same machine; the review concludes that only limited data suggest strip use decreases overdose rates or mortality.
